narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you; you finished in the third decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth.

Your LSAT score was the second most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 37, your score sits almost exactly at the average of students who received offers, so it helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately, the two weaker class rankings carried more weight than this solid LSAT performance.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 was below the 3.23 average of accepted students, your middle-income background is fairly common among applicants, and neither your gender nor race played any role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining years so that your class rank moves closer to the middle of your cohort. Retaking the LSAT to increase your score above 37 could also help offset the earlier decile rankings. Consider reapplying once you have stronger evidence of consistent academic achievement.
